title: Given a sorted array of numbers and a target sum, find a pair of elements whose values add up exactly to the target and return their indices. Solve it with the two-pointer technique. (LeetCode: Two Sum II: Input Array Is Sorted)
shortTitle: Pair with Target Sum (Two Pointers on a Sorted Array)
keyPoints: Place one pointer at the start and one at the end of the sorted array, then squeeze inward based on the current sum.
If the sum is too large, move the right pointer left to decrease it; if too small, move the left pointer right to increase it.
Each step eliminates one element permanently, so the algorithm runs in O(n) time with O(1) space.
The sorted order is the precondition that makes each comparison eliminate a candidate conclusively.
If the array is not sorted, sorting first costs O(n log n); a hash-map approach runs in O(n) without sorting.
LeetCode Two Sum II returns one-based indices, so add one to each zero-based index before returning.
This two-pointer pattern generalizes to three-sum, four-sum, and closest-sum variants.

s1_definition.oneliner: In a sorted array, start with pointers at both ends, then squeeze inward: too big means shrink the right, too small means grow the left.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Two-pointer technique** – place `left` at index 0 and `right` at the last index of a sorted array, then move them toward each other.
- **Sum comparison** – compute `arr[left] + arr[right]`; if it equals the target, return both indices; if it exceeds the target, decrement `right`; if it falls short, increment `left`.
- **Correctness** – the sorted order ensures that when the sum is too large, `right` can never be part of the answer with this `left`, so it is safely discarded.
- **Complexity** – O(n) time because each element is visited at most once; O(1) extra space.
- **Precondition** – the array must be sorted for the two-pointer elimination logic to work.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh at the National Bank of India has a sorted list of pending settlement amounts and needs to find exactly two settlements that together clear a target obligation. Instead of checking every possible pair, Priya stands at the smallest amount and Rajesh at the largest. If their two amounts add up to more than the target, Rajesh steps down. If they add up to less, Priya steps up. They walk toward each other until the two amounts hit the target exactly.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The pair-with-target-sum problem asks you to find two elements in a sorted array whose values add up to a given target, and the clean solution is the two-pointer technique that runs in O(n) time and O(1) space. You place one pointer at the start and one at the end, compute the sum of the two values they point to, and move the pointers inward based on whether the sum is too large or too small.

The core insight is the sorted order. When the current sum exceeds the target, the only way to make it smaller is to move the right pointer inward to a smaller value, and you can safely discard the old right element because pairing it with anything to the left would only make the sum larger. When the sum falls short, you move the left pointer for the same reason in reverse. Each step permanently eliminates one element, so every element is touched at most once.

In Rajesh's work at the National Bank of India, the clearing system returns outstanding settlement amounts in sorted order, and the regulator sometimes requires showing that a specific target obligation can be cleared by combining exactly two transactions. A brute-force pair check over hundreds of thousands of transactions would miss the settlement window, so the two-pointer sweep gives the answer in a single linear pass.

The senior-level point is about preconditions. The two-pointer method depends on the array being sorted. If the input is not sorted, you either sort it first at O(n log n) cost or switch to a hash-map approach that runs in O(n) without sorting. Choosing between those depends on whether the data arrives sorted and whether you need the original indices, and being explicit about that tradeoff separates someone who memorized a trick from someone who understands when to use it.

Remember one sentence: start with pointers at both ends of a sorted array and squeeze inward, moving the pointer that makes the sum closer to the target each step.
